subject: Media Literacy
title: False Balance
description: A short lesson to help you apply False Balance.

hook.text: A TV debate on climate change features one scientist and one denier. It looks balanced. But 97% of scientists agree.

buildup.text: False balance is giving equal time to unequal positions, making a fringe view seem as valid as scientific consensus.

discovery.text: It emerged from the journalistic habit of 'hearing both sides' — even when one side lacks evidence.

twist.text: False balance doesn't inform. It confuses audiences into thinking settled questions are still open debates.

climax.text: Balance means proportional representation of evidence, not equal time for unequal claims.

punchline.text: Two sides doesn't mean two equal sides.

quiz.question: What is false balance in journalism?
options: Covering only one side of a story
Giving equal time to positions with vastly unequal evidence
